utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric. Yesterday, before we adjourned, we talked about your first information that you submitted to the command about the situation with the morale in the 2nd Bosnian Brigade and about the things that you had found in place when you assumed the post. We are talking about the situation that you found in the 2nd Posavina Brigade. Once you informed the command about the situation, did the command decide to draft a more detailed information about the causes that had a direct bearing on the situation with morale and relationships in the 2nd Posavina Brigade, and who was tasked with drafting this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a decision was indeed made at the level of the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. The body that I was the head of was tasked with drafting such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: According to the authorities and the competencies of the body for morale and religious and legal affairs, was that your obligation, as the person who was at the head of that body?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. Besides me, there was just another legal officer in the body, and another officer who was in charge of civilian issues. So as regards the drafting of this information, I had to do most of it, because I was an assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how did you obtain information, how did you get by the knowledge that you later on incorporated into your report?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to draft such a report that would reflect the real situation as regards the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, I used the best method of work that was available to me at the time. That means that I would go directly to all the infantry battalions, to all the independent units which were on the strength of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and I talked to the most responsible persons in those units, starting with their commanders and their assistants, especially those in charge of moral guidance and security, and very often, in agreement with the assistants for morale guidance of these units, I also used those moments when the men of certain units were supposed to relieve other men who were on the first front lines, to talk with them about the problems that were visible in their units. Then I would draft notes and I would thus obtain information as to how the last men in the unit thought about the situation that was in place in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you were drafting this information, this document, did other members of the command participate in the drafting of this information? If so, could you then tell us who those people were who, together with you, participated in the drafting of this information.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was doing this work - and I must say that I had to invest a lot of effort to reach every unit and to carry out all these talks - and when this information was prepared in its, so to say, roll version, then a Working Group was assigned by the command, who was supposed to provide certain input into that information and help me to prepare this information in the most correct way. Members of this Working Group were Mr. Marko Tubakovic, who was the assistant commander for replenishment and personnel affairs in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and I believe that it was in his job description to do that, because he was the one who had a lot of contact with the units on the ground. And there was also Mr. Jovo Savic, a captain, who was a member of the operative educational body, and also a member of the staff of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In what month were you given the task to prepare this information, and during which months did you work on the drafting of this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got this task in late October, once I drafted my first information that I wrote based on the first time I saw the situation. Having realised that this called for a more elaborate analysis that would show what had a bearing on the morale of the 2nd Infantry Brigade, the command decided that this information indeed should be drafted, and I dedicated most of the time to drafting this information during the months of October and November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, this information, or this document, rather, was it a subject of any discussion by the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document was the subject of discussion, and let me first tell you: I personally drafted this information, taking into account certain suggestions by my colleagues from the Working Group, and this material that was drafted by me and my Working Group was read to the command of the 2nd Infantry Brigade. All the members of the command were present and they discussed this information that they had just heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P127 ter put before Mr. Zaric. This is the information, i.e., the document that we have just been talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while we are waiting for this exhibit, can you please tell us: When was this information adopted?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was adopted in late November or, to be more precise, on the 29th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this information very briefly, and then we will talk about the discussions that ensued and the way this information was adopted. Can you please tell us if this is that information.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the information that I drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who were the people present at the session of the command when the discussion took place about this information and when this information was adopted?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the information was being adopted as a document, with the conclusions that arose from the discussion, that session of the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was attended by the following people: On behalf of the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps, as our Superior Command, there were two assistant commanders of the Eastern Bosnia Corps. One of them was my immediate superior, according to my subordination line. That was Colonel Zivko Dosen. And the other one, the other assistant who also participated in this discussion was Colonel Dragan Jakovljevic, who was assistant commander of the Eastern Bosnia Corps for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify one thing. What was Zivko Dosen's role?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko Dosen was assistant commander of East Bosnia Corps for morale, guidance, religious, and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which members of the command were present when the information was discussed and adopted?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people who put their signature on this information were present, and the only person who was absent was Captain Milojevic, who was the assistant commander for logistics. He had participated in previous discussions, but on that particular day he was absent, for certain reasons, and I believe that there was another member of the command who was absent. He was the assistant chief of security. All in all, there were 13 of us who signed this information, who had participated in the discussion and who had drafted the conclusions that you can see at the end of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you please look at the last page of this document. Was it decided by the command that all the present -- on behalf of the command should sign this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was decided that all the members of the command should sign this information. We're talking about the army, so there was no voting, as one would have at a political forum. When the discussion ended, a proposal was heard and put forward that all the members of the command should put their signature on this information and thus support what is contained in this information, and this is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did all the members of the command who were present there personally sign this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All to the last signed this information, and all the members of the command really eagerly, and in the most responsible and constructive way, participated in the discussion, so that the fact that they put their signature and supported this information gives this information the character that it has.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you please look at number 3, where it says "the command of the brigade." Can you please read what it says under number 3. Is that you, and is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is me and this is my own signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how was this document which was adopted at the session of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade evaluated by your superior officers? I'm referring primarily to Mr. Zivko Dosen, who was your immediate superior, as regards the organ for morale, religious, and legal affairs?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information was evaluated with a very good evaluation by Mr. Dosen and Mr. Jakovljevic. Our command passed a test of maturity and humaneness by speaking out in the way that it did in this document. Perhaps I'm being immodest, but I know because I participated at a meeting in the East Bosnia Corps, where the commander himself, General Simic, and others who took part in the debate, referred to this document of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, mentioning it as an example of how other units should have the strength to speak out in public about the morale of the soldiers of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did the command decide to do? No. I withdraw this question. Just tell us: To whom was this information sent?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information had the character of a confidential document. In its original form, it was submitted to the Superior Command, that is, directly to the command of the East Bosnia Corps, which then had its headquarters in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did the command decide as to how this information should be used in the future?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command decided that this information should be forwarded, or rather, that all the soldiers in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade should be acquainted with the content of this information, in a reasonable manner. And I must say that two or three days after this information was adopted, a meeting was held in Obudovac which was attended by all the commanders of the infantry units and the independent units, their assistants for morale and security, and I was also at this meeting. So was Chief Milan Josic, and part of the meeting was attended by the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, Mr. Mile Beronja. At this meeting, we informed all those present about the positions taken by the command, about the situation we had found, and we gave all these men the task, because we considered them to be most responsible for the situation in their units, of transmitting this information and these evaluations to the soldiers, without referring to the original text of the information, but simply saying that this was one of the documents debated at the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. In its original form, the document was not forwarded to lower-level units as a confidential document, because we did not want it to give rise to other kinds of reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did the command decide that this document, that is, this information, should be forwarded to the representatives of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no mention of this, but it was decided that the representatives of the civilian authorities should be informed about certain standpoints which were expressed both in this document and in the debate that was held, and part of the information that was crucial for the people then in power in the municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what happened after this information about the situation as regards morale was adopted and signed at the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that after a few days I was sincerely disappointed to a certain extent because the original text of this document, as far as I was able to learn, was taken by Commander Beronja, although we hadn't agreed that this should be done and had acquainted Mr. Milan Simic and Mr. Todorovic with this document, and he was accompanied by a man who was working in the command for replenishment and personnel affairs and who was not a member of the command but was an influential man in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was a meeting held, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Between the command and the representatives of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right away, because the disclosure of certain matters from this document, as was unfortunately done by our commander, reverberated like a bomb that had exploded in our small area, and right away a meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who convened that meeting, and where was it held?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the meeting was called by the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and the meeting was held in Pelagicevo, in one of the rooms there. And the commander invited the representatives of the authorities from the Samac Crisis Staff and people from the authorities in Pelagicevo, as an integral part of the municipality under formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was the meeting attended by all the members of the command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be absolutely certain that they were all there, but 90 per cent of us members of the command were certainly present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And was the meeting attended by some commanders of the infantry battalions from the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The battalion commanders were there, and the commanders of the independent units. So this was an important meeting of the most important people from the military, and also the most responsible people from the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who of the representatives of the civilian authorities of Bosanski Samac attended the meeting? Can you enumerate the names?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the representatives of the authorities, there was Mr. Blagoje Simic, as the president of the Crisis Staff; Milan Simic, as the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac municipality; then there was Stevan Todorovic, as the chief of the public security station of the municipality of Bosanski Samac; there was Mr. Savo Popovic, as a member of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Samac; there was Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who at that time -- I don't know whether he was a member of the War Presidency. I'm not sure of that. But I know he did attend the meeting, if in no other capacity than as the chief of the ministry department for National Defence at the level of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Along with all these gentlemen, there was also a guest who had arrived with Mr. Todorovic and whose name was Ostoja Minic. He introduced himself as a High Representative of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you can recollect, was the meeting also attended by Simeon Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I'm not a hundred per cent certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who chaired and presided over the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by our commander, the commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, Major Mile Beronja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who took part in the debate at this meeting? Primarily I mean the representatives of the civilian authorities who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well that the discussion included a brief intervention by Mr. Blagoje Simic, but he was not among the first to speak from the civilian authorities, and a very long polemic and discussion was conducted by Mr. Milan Simic, as the representative of the Executive Board, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, as the chief of the public security station; and to our great surprise, Mr. Ostoja Minic, who had arrived as a guest and introduced himself as a High Representative of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember whether Mr. Bozo Ninkovic took part in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bozo Ninkovic also took part in the discussion, and on behalf of the brigade command, there was a brief discussion by the commander, who made a few brief comments. Then the Chief of Staff and one of the battalion commanders, Mr. Savo Bosic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you recall, after all this time has elapsed, what Mr. Blagoje Simic said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, Blagoje Simic was the most sensitive to the fact that this information touched upon political issues, and he felt that the command and the military should not be dealing with these issues. He thought it was not proper for the military to give political assessments, and that's what he mostly complained about, because he felt that this could upset the relationship between politics and the military as a defence component. This was the most serious criticism put forward by Mr. Blagoje Simic at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have already said that Stevan Todorovic also took part in the discussion at that meeting. First of all, tell me: What state was Mr. Todorovic in at that meeting? Could something be noticed on him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to say, and it doesn't refer just to Mr. Todorovic, that it was sad to see in what state Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Milan Simic, and Mr. Ostoja Minic, who introduced himself as a High Representative, were in. They were more than drunk, without any feeling of responsibility for what was said at that meeting which, in my view, was very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us briefly what Stevan Todorovic said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic evidently had at his disposal information as to who might be the author of the document, regardless of the fact that there were 13 signatories to the document. He used the word -- rather, he said that the KGB system could be seen in this document, the KGB was the secret service of the former Soviet Union and part of the Yugoslav UDBA, U-D-B-A. He was alluding to the fact that I was the author of this document, and he wanted to say that it was something that any person should condemn rather than giving it its proper weight. He said that there were many insinuations, lies, that there was slander in the document. He said that these were Stalinist methods. These were very harsh words. He felt that this was some kind of military putsch, that it was to bring into question the existing authorities in the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have already said what kind of state Mr. Milan Simic was in. Can you tell us briefly what Mr. Milan Simic said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Milan Simic was very arrogant. I had never seen him in that light before. He supported the approach of Mr. Todorovic as to the way in this information was drawn up and what its outlines were. And then he addressed all of us in the command in a very cynical manner. He said we had to bear in mind, because the army was dependent on them - and when I say "them," I meant the authorities - so he said if the Executive Board, and I and my men don't bring cigarettes to the soldiers on the line, if we don't bring them food, how do you think you will survive? And this caused a lot of bitterness and outrage, so that one of the commanders who was present and who had a lot of authority in the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and that was Mr. Savo Bosic, who was the commander of the 1st Infantry Battalion, which was part of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. He spoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what Mr. Savo Bosic said on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Bosic said to Mr. Simic, first of all, you should have arrived at this meeting in a normal state and not drunk. Secondly, he told him that it was very sad that the first man of the executive government should have such an arrogant attitude toward his own army, because we were an army originating from that area. In the morning we were defending the lines; in the afternoon we were working on the fields and in the factories. So Mr. Bosic responded to this very primitive reaction by Mr. Milan as a representative of the executive government in the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Sir, at some point you mentioned Mr. Simic. Were you thinking of Mr. Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was thinking of Mr. Milan Simic, as the president of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what Bozo Ninkovic said at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bozo Ninkovic introduced himself as being the representative, and in fact he was one, of the ministry of the National Defence of the Republika Srpska, and as chief of the department, stating that, according to him, there were some elements and that the army, in spite of the laws of the National Defence, was mixing itself in other competencies which were not its place. He didn't have any particular arguments to support this theory, but I would say that in this litany of critics of this choir of people who came to tell us various things, he was just basically supporting all the complaints that the other ones were formulating.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please tell us, according to your recollection: How did Ostoja Minic behave and what did he say at the meeting in question? And I'm thinking of that man who was representing the Ministry of the Interior of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a story on its own, I must say. I saw him for the first time then. Even though he introduced himself as being some kind of an inhabitant of Donja Dubica, that he was born in the municipality of Odzak, that he was a compatriot, he was so drunk that it was incredible. But he very openly, very openly and in a way was a very destructive conversation, he said and started to threaten, stating that this material is a criminal act and that he directly -- or that it directly criticises constitutional order of the Republika Srpska, and stating that he had the occasion to control the work of the security station and that many things that were said as an indicational way, because in that context the information was not talking about the authors of these actions, but it just stated the actions. He said that the security post was working well, and accordingly to the law, that there's nothing illegal going on at that security station. And he was a member of a work group which represented the Ministry of the Interior, and this work group came even before and after on the territory covered by the security station. Now, as to what was found in that security station, we've heard Mr. Slavko Paleksic, who testified before this Honourable Court, and I believe that everything was said through him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You told us who were the members who took part in this conversation, but did you, Mr. Zaric, take part in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, in spite of the fact that I was trying to find my words, or find words from my commander - I was sitting right next to him. I was sitting to his left side, and to his right side, the chief of the staff, Mr. -- Captain Josic was there, Major Beronja was his name, and he didn't allow me to talk because he said that it was not a good moment to speak. The atmosphere was not good, and that is why I shouldn't be defending the -- whatever this information was stating. So that's why I must say that the command did not have its chance and the members of the command did not get a chance to explain to these men who represented the authorities to say what was our purpose, why was this information written. Maybe I'm not being modest, but I am one -- I was one of the most influential people who worked on the drafting of this information. I was never given the chance to even say a word during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us: How many times did you ask the commander to give you the possibility to speak or to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a few times, three times, actually. Whenever these men from the authorities would take the floor and they would evaluate us the way they were, I thought that it was very important to show and to explain what were the purposes why and how we got these informations which were stated in this document called the information. And in spite of the fact that I myself wanted to participate in this meeting, I was not given a chance to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how did this meeting end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting ended, I would say, in an atmosphere which was resembling the Far West.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe to us what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Ostoja Minic, who was a man who introduced himself as being a High Representative of an organ of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska, he said some very heavy words and he was insulting the command. He was saying that it was our responsibility to -- for if a putsch would occur and we should expect that the authorities would change. And the other members of the command had a very strong opinion also, but Mr. Jovan Erletic entered in a sort of a verbal duel with him. He was a member of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade and he was present. So he was the one who had this verbal duel with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly? This meeting basically was not fruitful; it did not bring out many conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this verbal duel, in the end, turned out to be a scene in which Mr. Minic got up, walked towards Mr. Erletic, and the latter is a very strong man, a very robust man, and he answered at that moment in such a way that he did not allow Mr. Minic to approach him and to grab him by the jacket. So he grabbed the other one and they started to push each other. There was some pushing and shoving and they were shoving each other on the wall. And I was more under the impression that we were in a restaurant of the Far West rather than at a very important meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this incident, did this meeting continue, or was it over?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was interrupted at that point. We each went on our merry way, and basically it just ended without any conclusion. And I think that given the seriousness and the character of the people who were present there, this meeting ended without a conclusion and without any serious messages that could objectively be given or be brought after such a serious meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After this meeting was ended, Mr. Zaric, tell me: Were there any procedures taken against you on behalf of some authorities of the civil authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this information and after this meeting, I was basically set aside from that very moment up until the end of the war. Some people from the authorities didn't really like me, and I don't -- I can't even tell you how lucky I am to be alive today and to be testifying here before this international criminal justice court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Defence of the Samac department, did they send some kind of a letter to the attention of the Eastern Corps, Eastern Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Right after, one or two days after the adoption of this information, a letter arrived. This letter was drafted on behalf of the department of the Ministry of Defence of Samac, and in this letter I was being degraded. This letter stated about the desertion of my son Mirel, who was 17 years old at the time. He was going to the fourth year of the gymnasium, and they were saying that I had some dubious contacts with some people on the municipality. And they suggested in this letter that the command of the brigade should think seriously about how exemplary or how recommended it is that such a man should be at such a high position within the command of the 2nd Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown the document D31/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please take this document and put it on the ELMO so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe we have some technical problems. We cannot see anything on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can go ahead, Mr. Pisarevic, because -- what the document is all about and then discuss it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We don't need to have it on the ELMO. We already have it, actually, because it's an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honour, it is not necessary, but I just thought that it would facilitate the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have read this document, you know its contents?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I will remember this document until I die.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us: Is there anything in this document that resembles the truth?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are all lies and defamations. There's not one single word of truth in this document. And as you can see, this document was forwarded to very important organs from the municipality and the territory of the East Bosnia Corps. And, according to Mr. Ninkovic, it was just to shed a very ugly light on my own person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Could you please tell us if this document was discussed during a meeting of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was discussed during a meeting of the command, and as a member of the command when this document was forwarded, I, as a member, insisted that the command should take positions regarding some evaluations of myself which were stated in this document. I wanted them either to support me or to condemn this disqualification or this way of behaviour. The command reacted in a very positive way, and they had written a letter back to the author of this text, Mr. Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show Mr. Zaric Document D32/4. That is a letter of the command of the 2nd Infantry Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please take a look at this document. We are not going to discuss the content, because the document speaks for itself. But just please confirm to us, if you can: Is this the document which is actually a letter, stemming from the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, forwarded to the Ministry of Defence of Posavina, department of Samac, and is this an answer to the letter sent by Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who was at the time chief of the ministry, the department of Ministry of Defence in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is a reaction to this letter. It is. This letter was sent from the command and this letter was sent to Mr. Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, is this written by a commander or does this stem from the command, as a general body?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comes from the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, but this document is signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do not need this document any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, the command of the East Bosnia Corps, did it take any measures with regard to this document or was it something that was discussed only by your own command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the command of the East Bosnia Corps did not take any particular measures once they received this information. They left it to us to deal with this internally, in our area of responsibility, to the best of our abilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you aware of the fact that there was a session of the Municipal Assembly of Samac municipality on the 16th of December, 1992, in the Trile restaurant in Pisari village?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of the fact, and I personally attended that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you attend that meeting? In what capacity? In what capacity did you attend the meeting that was held on the 16th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the authority of the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, Major Beronja, to go to that meeting. It was also in the description of my job. It was more normal for the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs to represent the command as a liaison officer between the command and the civilian bodies. Very often times I was bypassed, but this time, Commander Beronja gave me his authority to attend the session which was held on the 16th of December, 1992, in Pisari village, in the well-known restaurant Trile, and that's how I went and participated in that session, as a guest, on behalf of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in brief outlines: What was discussed at that session and whether the information drafted by the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was considered at that session, and was it in any way discussed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were several items on the agenda, and this information, as a document, was not on the agenda; at least, I didn't see it. However, there was another evaluation of security and political situation that was elaborated by a document drafted by the Crisis Staff. This was one item on the agenda and this was the information that was discussed and which gave the tone to the entire session which was held on the 16th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, although you were only a guest at that session, were you given an opportunity to take the floor and address the deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was given that opportunity. I was given the opportunity to speak. I can only say that one of the participants in the discussion was the former or the first president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, Mr. Mirko Jovanovic. And when we considered the evaluation of the security and political situation, that was done on the basis of a particular bulletin, and my name was mentioned as one of the first traitors of the Serbian people and the author of some dubious material. Then I received attacks from the most responsible persons from the government; however, I tried to contribute in my own style and I tried to explain what was treated by the information that I authored. However, my impression was that my words did not penetrate the minds and the conscience of the deputies of Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who were the deputies who portrayed you as a traitor of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that the information was presented in a bulletin, with particular iconography, and that was signed by Mr. Blagoje Simic. Who were other people who supported that text, I wouldn't go into that, but I know that at that session, the attacks on me were by Mr. Milan Simic, by Mr. Stevan Todorovic, Aco Jankovic, especially Mr. Simeun Simic and also Mr. Blagoje Simic, who said that I engaged in politics while I worked in the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There are two words missing here. When Mr. Zaric was talking about Mr. Blagoje Simic, he said also in the milder form. This is what we heard of what Mr. Zaric said. I don't see this in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is that line 20 or line 19?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's page -- it's page 22, line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can clear the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you were talking about the people who participated in that session, and you mentioned that Mr. Blagoje Simic also spoke. Tell us: What did you say a little while ago? How did Mr. Blagoje Simic talk about you and about the information that you authored?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was recognisable at that session, and the way I had seen and perceived Blagoje Simic, he did not participate in many discussions. However, he always protected the political core, and in that meeting he also pointed to the fact that either I or the command of the brigade interfered too much in politics. And according to him, this was not the task of the army. That was his opinion. And I was given the chance to react, and I said that his words were too harsh and that this is not what the army did. And that is the only thing that he said. He talked about the political engagement. If the Trial Chamber deems it necessary for me to say what other participants said, I will gladly do that and you will become aware how much calmer and milder Mr. Blagoje Simic was with respect to the other participants in the discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was his position milder than the position of other participants in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. His position was much, much milder. However, when he presented this political differentiation, he was talking to me and he was addressing me, and he didn't attack me as much as the others did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you aware of the fact that some deputies of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, who were SDS members, who didn't agree with the discussion and the overall politics, walked out of that assembly and the SDS party? Are you aware of the fact? Do you remember that? And if you do, can you tell us who these people were.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember two cases. One was -- involved Mr. Milan Jekic, who at the beginning of the war was the assistant commander of the police station in Bosanski Samac. Formerly he had been an SDS deputy. At that particular session of the assembly, he publicly voiced his disagreement with the policy of the Serbian Democratic Party and the words of some people who participated in that discussion, and he said that from then on he should not be considered a member of the SDS and he would no longer come to any of the sessions of the assembly. As far as I know, Mr. Jekic didn't go back on these words. The second participant in that discussion who was very critical against Mr. Milan Simic and the work of the Executive Board was Mr. David Simic who was also a deputy and a member of the Serbian Democratic Party. However, later on I heard that he did not abandon his seat in the assembly and that he remained a member of the assembly. But at that particular moment, he was very negative towards some of the moves by the Executive Board and by Mr. Milan Simic, who at that time was the head of that body.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At that session, what did Mr. Mirko Jovanovic say? He was the former president of the Executive Board of the Samac municipality and the president of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Question posed by Mr. Pisarevic was not properly recorded. The question was: "At that session, what happened to Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, former president of the municipal board -- Executive Board," I'm sorry. The question was not: What did Mr. Mirko Jovanovic say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let's just have the question posed again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what do you know about -- what happened at that session to Mr. Mirko Jovanovic, the former president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Samac, who, at the same time, was the president of the Executive Board of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Samac municipality and Pelagicevo under formation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic was given an opportunity to say for the first time before the highest body as to how he had been removed from his position as the president of the Executive Board, and for what reasons. He thought that this was an illegitimate act, and he said that some move that had been taken at the beginning, in the early days of the war, were not the moves that he, as the president of the Executive Board, could have seconded. His attendance of the funeral of Aleksandar Vuk, a Special, who was killed on the 1st of May of 1992, from which he couldn't return because of certain problems, that is, the corridor in the area of Brcko municipality was cut off, he was late, and that was used as a reason for the people in the government to believe that he did not want to go on performing his tasks. He said that he didn't want to leave the Serbian Democratic Party. He said that within his abilities, he would continue fighting for some of the goals. And as far as I know, Mirko Jovanovic, either that year or in the following year, he became a deputy in the peoples assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to my learned friend. Intervention to the transcript with regard to the interpretation. It's page 25, line 13. Mr. Zaric said: "Before the highest legislative body," I believe, and we heard that. And the other issue, maybe my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic can clarify whether Mr. Zaric is speaking on the legislative body on the municipal level or it's a higher level, in order to clarify that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: First of all we deal with the omission of the legislative body. Do you accept what Mr. Pantelic has said, that you had said it was before the highest legislative body?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's all right. The second part where Mr. Pantelic wants to clarify, you can clarify that with Mr. Simo Zaric, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you said "the highest legislative body," were you referring to the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac being the highest legislative body on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's precisely what I meant to that. I meant that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as Mr. Zaric has already mentioned the bulletin that was published, I would ask that Exhibit D29/4 be put in front of him. This is the bulletin in which the role of Mr. Zaric was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please have a look at the document before you put it on the ELMO. Have you seen it? First tell us, Mr. Zaric: What is this bulletin?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This bulletin is one of the ways in which the public was provided with information about the assessments made by the people in the authorities, or rather, what the authorities felt the people should be informed about. There were many such bulletins published during the war, and the chief ideologues and editors of everything contained in these bulletins were Mr. Simic and Mr. Bozo Ninkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you mentioned Simic. Since we have had many people in these proceedings with the last name of Simic, could you tell us his first name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said Simeun Simic. I said Mr. Simeun Simic. I don't know whether it entered the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So the person is Mr. Simeun Simic, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's Mr. Simeun Simic, and I think that the title of this bulletin deserves attention. I wish to draw everyone's attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please tell us: Is this a regular issue of the bulletin or is it a special issue?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a special issue, and here in the middle it says that it's a special issue. And it was specially published for the first assembly of the municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation, which was held on the 16th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, would you please turn to page 3. I think it's page 3, where your name is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Before we do that, Mr. Zaric had stated a couple of lines before, I think it was lines 16 and 17 on page 27, that he thought that the title of the bulletin deserved attention. Perhaps, Mr. Zaric, you could tell us what the title is and why it deserves attention before Mr. Pisarevic moves on with his next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would the usher please help me, because I don't know how to work this equipment. It should be moved a little bit. If you can move it up a bit. The first thing I want to say is that this is a special issue, and here in the middle, that's what it says, that it's a special issue. This large title here says: "Enemies don't have a chance." This is the chief political message of this bulletin. And on the right and left, it mentions the assessment of the security situation in the municipality. Because of this phrase here, which is so evident on the front page, and the fact that it's a special issue, I think this has a certain weight, especially if you look at pages 2 and 3, and there you can see something connected to my name, and some other people who are called to task in this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could Mr. Zaric be so kind to read the full title the -- of this bulletin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I'm sure he can read that, because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. [Interpretation] No, Mr. Zaric. Just the topic, the topic. You don't have to read every word. What it says here in a slanting line, could you read out the whole title, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The writing says: "Political and security situation in the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before you look at the page I wanted you to look at, would you please tell me: Did this bulletin have the character of a means of information in the municipality of Samac in 1992 and 1993? Was it part of the media, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. And I don't know in how many copies it was printed, but there were enough to reach all the institutions in the municipality and the soldiers, the ranks. So it was a means of information until conditions were created for a proper newspaper, which was called Corridor, later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who published this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the bulletin of the Crisis Staff, as the highest legislative body in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think it's time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please look at this document which is before you, the bulletin. Can you tell us whether your name is mentioned here and whether it says that you are neither a deputy nor a member of any assembly body?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page number 2 of this bulletin, the middle paragraph, there is a sentence which reads as follows: "The fact that this is a strange session of the assembly is also shown by the fact that the agenda contains some material authored by Simo Zaric, who is neither a deputy nor a member of any assembly organ."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Where it says "material," do you understand this to mean the information drawn up by the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the material mentioned in the bulletin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, would you look at the signature at the bottom of the page. What does it say here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the signature, it says "president of the War Presidency of the municipality of Samac, Dr. Blagoje Simic," and there is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is there also a stamp? If you can read it. If it's not legible, don't try. It's not really very legible.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, obviously this is the stamp of the Crisis Staff, because I can see that it mentions the Municipal Assembly. But I don't see the entire text. I see that part of it says "Samac," so I assume this is the official stamp then used by the Crisis Staff for its needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We no longer need this document. Mr. Zaric, did you suffer any consequences after learning of the existence of this information and after this bulletin was published? Did you continue holding the post of the assistant commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs in the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed on until the autumn of 1993, when I was definitely replaced and assigned to the duty of a private in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, as a private in the army of Republika Srpska, where did you go to the war theatre?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in quite a few places, from Han Pijesak, in the direction of Zepa, on Majevica, in Bosansko Grahovo, in Krupa, in Glamoc, in Drvar, and there is no part of the war front in the area of responsibility of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade where I was not with the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. And throughout this time, you were a common private in the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A common private, although I had an officer's rank. I was commanded by common privates or by sergeants. But I didn't mind. All I wanted was to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, do you have any information about the arrest of Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic by the military police from Brcko, that is, from the East Bosnia Corps of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the arrest of Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this was sometime in the first half of November 1992. The members of the military security of the East Bosnia Corps, or rather, their representatives, acting through the military police on the territory of the municipality of Brcko, arrested Mr. Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic, for certain reasons I was not aware of, and this, of course, gave rise to reactions by certain political structures and some members of the renegade forces. And a part of the road passing through the territory in the direction of Bijeljina and Brcko was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The cutting off of the corridor, where it did happen? In the area of what municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the territory of the municipality of Samac, at two points. One was at the crossroads in Crkvina, where part of the road leads in the direction of Modrica, and further on, in the direction of the western part of Republika Srpska; and the other part of the road leads in the direction of Gradacac. The other large point where a bottleneck was created to prevent people from using the corridor, this was on the road to Gradacac, near the village of Kornica, where the road turns left to the village of Gornja Slatina. It was at this crossroads that the barricade was set up, blocking passage along that communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you be a bit more precise as to which forces took part in the closing off of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was unfortunately a participant of this drama. When we talk about the corridor of Crkvina and the stopping of people to cross were members of the Special Forces, they wore camouflage uniforms, they had hats on their heads. We couldn't see their faces. And there was a member -- there were members of the special force, and they were in the direction of Kornica, going towards Gornja Slatina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you talk about members of Special Forces, who are these people?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By closing off the corridor, we knew that Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was leading that action, and he was also accompanied by Mr. Slobodan Miljkovic, Lugar. He was his fateful assistant. And there were also some other people with them, some volunteers who had come at the time from Serbia to our territory. And there were some local members of the Special Forces who in them saw their heroes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you have an encounter with these people who were on these barricades which, through the corridor, was cut? If you did have any contacts, please tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a direct contact, first in Crkvina in a car in which I was. At that point, it was in the afternoon hours and I was going in the direction of Pelagicevo. I was headed to the command in Pelagicevo, where I was the assistant of the commander for morale, religious, and legal affairs. I was also accompanied by at the time by Captain Jovo Savic. He was also a member of that command. We were stopped at the point by an officer of the police station, Mr. Tesic Djordje. He came by car, and behind him we could see four or five special members, members of the Special Forces. They were armed to the teeth. They had hats on their heads and we couldn't know who was there. We didn't recognise them. We didn't know who they were, who was hiding behind these uniforms. Mr. Djordje approached us and told us: Where are you coming from? How come you came here? They have the task to kill you. I was so surprised, and I was so astonished by this, and by such a reaction of Mr. Djordje Tesic, whom I had known as a very serious police officer, because before the war he also worked for a certain period of time on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. To be more precise, in Osijek. And because of the war before -- because of problems before the war, he came to Samac and became a professional police officer at the police station of Samac. He only said the following: Turn around and run away before Lugar shows up.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you and Mr. Jovo Savic do at that point?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was driving the car. I did not have time to think. I was under the impression that this was no joke. We turned around and we went back where we came from. We went in the direction of Bosanski Samac, and from that crossroad, all the way up until Bosanski Samac and up until the building in which I live, there's approximately 4 kilometres. That's the distance between the crossroads and my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have other encounters of the sort?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening we hid in such a way that it would look like it was an event from a film. We noticed that in Samac arrived a car. Some people were inside that car and they had special uniforms. They wore these special hats. And we went around that settlement, that part of the town, and very quickly we were able to put the car in the garage and to enter my apartment building, the number 4, the entrance number 4 of that apartment building, and we were following from upstairs and we could see them drive around, because we couldn't understand what had happened to us, to me and Captain Savic. We had spent all that night awake. We stayed up, and we were ready that should they enter the apartment building, we were ready to fight back with weapons in order to save our lives. But that night, nobody came into that building, into my building. Nobody came into that entrance, since Mr. Savic and myself were awake and we were watching to see what was going on around the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Jovo Savic, Captain Jovo Savic and yourself, what did you do in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early morning hours, around 6.00 a.m., as soon as daytime came, we thought the situation became more or less normal, so Mr. Savic and myself drove in the direction -- through Crkvina in the direction of Kornica. And what's interesting to say here is that that morning, in Crkvina, there were no patrol cars, there was no checkpoint, and we thought that the situation had gone back to normal. But around 6.30 a.m., we arrived to the second checkpoint, where we could see a tank, a Praga, some military vehicles. The situation was horrifying. We saw, on the road that goes from Gornja Slatina towards the crossroads, that there were dozens and dozens of various vehicles, from trucks to buses. Everything was blocked. And near that crossroads, as we were going from Crkvina to the crossroad, we -- Mr. Vincetic got into our car. I remember that last name because the son of that Vincetic died, and that's why that man had gone from Obudovac, and he asked us if we could give him a ride. When we approached the crossroad, all of a sudden Captain Savic said: Look, there's Lugar with his team, with his group of people, at the crossroad. And we were at that point approximately 50 to 70 metres away of the crossroad. I stopped my car, and to the right-hand side, Captain Savic saw, from that house where we had stopped, his wife was born in that house and this is where her parents lived. So we thought that maybe it was a good idea to stop and to very calmly go and pay them a visit. It was his in-laws. And we thought that maybe we can have a coffee and think and see, evaluate how Mr. Lugar would react, and all these volunteers who were armed to the teeth and who were, all them, aside from Lugar or two or three men, wore these camouflage uniforms and these hats, and we couldn't see who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed there about half an hour. We had coffee. We were looking out the window to see what the situation was like. The situation did not change. And then we evaluated that it would be a good idea to get in the car and go on our way, because we thought that Mr. Lugar would come with his group of people, because they were very attentive to our car and they were very often looking at the car and in our direction. So we got in the car. I was driving for about 20 to 30 metres, and all of a sudden, in the direction of the car, that police officer, Djordje Tesic, who had told us the previous evening to stop, or who had stopped us at the crossroad in Crkvina, and behind him, Mr. Lugar was walking in the middle of the road, and to the left, as well as to the right, he was accompanied by five special members, and they were dressed in such a way as I already described to you. Their weapons were pointing at us, and they all started heading in the direction of the car in which we were, and that I stopped. Mr. Tesic, Djordje, only said the following: Gentlemen, you are under arrest. And from this moment on, you will have to go to the base in Hrvatska Tisina. I only asked: Who gave such an order, and who can give such an order? At which point, Mr. Lugar came to us by car, so he approached us, and I must say that he is very particular. I'm not going to describe him to you. He is very cynical. When you look at him, you fear. So he came close to me. He was about 20 centimetres away from me. He looked inside the car. He saw Captain Savic. He also noticed Mr. Vincetic, whom he probably didn't even know. And he said: Look at my little birds. They came me on their own. As if we were some little birds, and as if we had flown into his nest. That's what he meant. So he said: Little birds, where are you flying to? Where are you going? That's what he said, in a very arrogant way. I tried to be very determined, and I said: I'm going to the command of the brigade. I'm going to work. He said: What command? Of which brigade, Mr. Zaric? And I said: Mr. Lugar, you know very well that I'm a member of the command and that I'm going to Pelagicevo. At that point -- and I just want to say this before: That when they started walking towards the car I said to Captain Savic not to move his hand or his arm. I didn't move either because I knew what the reaction would have been. If they wanted to kill us, I thought that it was sufficient to make a wrong move and they would have pierced the car with bullets. We just stayed calm, and I believe that this is what helped us not to get killed at that time. Now, to the right-hand side of me where Mr. Jovo Savic was sitting, he was also approached by one of these men who were wearing a camouflage uniform. And when this other guy saw Savic, he said: Uncle, what are you doing there? When he said something, he recognised that it's Mihajcic, who is a member of his family and who was wearing this camouflage uniform. So when he said "Uncle," this calmed Mr. Lugar down. And so he said, literally, the following: Gentlemen, go directly to Pelagicevo. I'm going to be there in half an hour from now and I want to find you at the command. We didn't say anything. I was only thinking whether I would get out of that situation alive and whether there would be no incident as the car leaves. Fortunately, there was no other incidents, there was no other measures taken towards us. The car just started, we turned left. And I must say that hundreds and hundreds of buses, trucks, and people were stopped on that road, and they -- it was very difficult to drive, but we went on through the right and we were able to go through and drive on. So we got to Donji Zabari, where at that point there was a forward command post of the East Bosnia Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So how did it end, this closing off of the corridor situation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jovo Savic and myself were in Donji Zabari and we found there the commander of the corps. He was already a general at the time, General Major Novica Simic. We told him what happened, and we asked him: How is it possible that someone should behave that way and close off a corridor? He told us that he was following the situation. He thinks that our commander, Beronja, was quite guilty for it. It was his fault. That's what he said at the time. But he also told us not to be scared to go to the command and that he informed about this the commander and General Mladic, as well as the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, Mr. Momir Talic, who was very soon supposed to send an armoured unit of his which was supposed to make sure that this corridor be reopened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in the end was the corridor reopened after a period of time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, during the day the corridor was reopened and an armoured unit, tank unit, bearing other means, arrived from the part of Odzak which is in the zone of responsibility there, who was headed by Colonel Dupljanin. And because of such an important number of men who arrived and because they were quite impressive, the people who had closed off the corridor, such as Crni, Lugar, and other special members, must have thought that they stand no chance and that it would not be a good idea to fight. And fortunately, through the intervention of Colonel Beronja, who went there on the premises, the barricades were removed, the special members were withdrawn, and the corridor was reopened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Mr. Todorovic and Mr. Milan Simic? Were they released from prison?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that several days later they were released. According to my information, they were taken to Bijeljina, where they were interrogated by the security organs, and later on, upon somebody's intervention, they were released and they were -- they returned to Bosanski Samac. And this contributed to the calming down of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what happened after that to those people, Crni, Lugar, and others who were in the area of Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, given the dramatic nature of that situation before the corridor was closed, information was available to us that a group of scouts from the 2nd Krajina Brigade had been illegally arrested. Their commander was Jovo Vukobrat and their area of responsibility was towards Gradacac, in that part. And these scouts had been arrested by Crni, Lugar, Captain Jez, who discharged the duties of the assistant commander of intelligence and security in the 2nd Posavina Brigade, unfortunately. And after the incident with the corridor, I suppose that this situation was taken the most of, and it seems that during the arrest of these scouts, one of them was killed in a very brutal manner and was hidden in a kiln by those who had killed him. And that's when Crni, Lugar, and their group of specials were arrested, among them was a person from the territory of Samac municipality. These people were taken to the remand centre of the military prison in Banja Luka, and later on proceedings were initiated against them by the military prosecutor and by the military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric. Now I would kindly ask you to tell us something about the events that have been mentioned by various witnesses before this Trial Chamber. The first thing I'd like to ask you is the following: Mr. Zaric, together with Teodor Tutnjevic, also known as Toso, were you ever in the police station in Bosanski Samac in the period between 18 April and 26 April 1992? I'm talking about an event which allegedly happened during the night.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was never in the public security station during the night. The longest period of my stay there was on the 26th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you familiar with any person whose nickname is Bokan?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of Bokan only from the media, from the newspapers. I believe that he belonged to some pro-Chetnik units. All I know about this person I read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in the police station in Bosanski Samac, did you ever see or were you present while somebody was cocking their pistol against Mr. Sulejman Tihic's head and fired in the air?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing like that ever happened before my eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Between the 17 April 1992 and the end of 1992, did you ever give an interview or did you ever participate in any radio show? When I said "interview," I meant whether you ever spoke to a journalist of Radio Samac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never gave any interviews. I never appeared on any shows on Radio Samac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever issue an order to anybody regarding their work obligation, either those in Bosanski Samac or in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. This was not my task. I did not have any reason to do that. All that was under the authority of the department of the Ministry of Defence, so anybody who says differently is lying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to go into private session because I'm going to mention some names of the witnesses who were protected before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know a citizen of Bosanski Samac by the name of Amir Dervic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Amir Dervic. We are nodding acquaintances. He is the brother of a Dervic whom I knew better. We used to call him Les. He worked in the public security centre, in the communications department, and that's how I also know the younger Dervic, his brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether Amir Dervic was a member of the 4th Detachment of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a member of the 4th Detachment, and his commander was Dzemal Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on the night between the 16th and the 17th April 1992, did you use a Motorola to communicate with Amir Dervic and did you issue orders to him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any Motorolas available to me. The only communication means that we had was Rupovka 12, and we used it to establish communication with the commander. So any story about Motorolas [Realtime transcript read in error "moment row las"], Rupovkas or any such thing is just a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one small clarification. It's not clear what the answer is here. "So any story about moment row las"; it's Motorolas, here on page 43, line 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps Mr. Zaric can just repeat what he said slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I did not have a Motorola. Motorolas were not at the time available to us. We did not have them at our disposal. And to be more precise, never during the war on the defence line of the town of Samac Motorolas were used as the means of communication among the men on the front line. We used a different means of communication. It was a very simple means of communication. We did not have Motorolas, and especially not on that morning that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you mentioned this wire connection. Let's clarify this a bit. What do you mean when you say: "We had a wire connection"? Wire means of communication.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, wire communication. When the line of defence was established, when trenches were dug and bunkers erected, and when trenches were traced for the army to move safely through, then we also established a wire connection. That means that we put a coil of wire on a little device that only had one receiver, and then when you turn this coil several times, then it starts ringing, and the next such device was a bit further, and another one a bit further, all along the trench. This was a direct link to the person who was the commander of that defence line. And every of these devices had its communication. So when somebody called, they would say: Can number 1 respond? And number 1 would respond. There was also number 2, number 3, and number 4. When the coil is turned, everybody's line is ringing, everybody picks up the receiver at the same time, but then the person calling has to identify the one whom he wants to respond. And vice versa: If the person on the line wanted to communicate with the base, they did the same thing. And that's how the communication was established. That is what we did in order for the army to communicate on the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, is that a classical telephone wire line?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a classical telephone wire line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This way of communication by way of classical telephone wire communication, could that be eavesdropped on? Could anybody in the enemy forces hear that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody could tap into that line. Nobody else could hear that communication. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to go into private session, because I'm going to mention a witness who testified here as a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.
