utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ask Stevan Todorovic, the chief of police in Bosanski Samac, to release some other people from detention, in addition to Tihic and Witness N?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, I did not conceal my dissatisfaction, and there was a constant verbal skirmish going on. I felt that people could not be arrested and deprived of their liberty without certain criteria being applied, and this is what Mr. Todorovic and the police were doing. He always said that I should not get involved with that, that he was in charge of that, so I was constantly, how shall I say it, trying to intervene verbally with Mr. Todorovic. And I remember well an incident when Mr. Esref Zaimbegovic, whom the Crisis Staff appointed in the beginning to be the coordinator in Utva, and I was -- no, in Uniglas, and I was encouraged by this, because when it so happened that when I went to see Mr. Simic in the Crisis Staff, Mr. Blagoje Simic, I would see Mr. Simic sitting in an office working with people, and Esref Zaimbegovic working in the next office as coordinator. And I thought that conditions were being created that were normal and that the situation would develop along those lines. But this lasted only for a brief period. And I have to say that I heard from people working in the crime detection service that not only there, but all the coordinators and all the directors were asked to provide lists of employees in those companies, and then Mr. Todorovic would evaluate from his own viewpoint who was where. And I know that he also detained Mr. Esref Zaimbegovic, who had an MA in economics and who was one of the best businessmen then residing on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us what the ethnicity of Mr. Zaimbegovic was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zaimbegovic was by ethnicity a Muslim, and I know that before the war he was the president of the municipal committee of the league of reformist forces, which was led at that time by Mr. Ante Markovic. That was his political affiliation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. At line -- sorry, page 49, line 8, Mr. Zaric said that: "In principle, I did not conceal my dissatisfaction and there was a constant verbal skirmish going on. I felt that people could not be arrested and deprived of their liberty without certain criteria being applied." In my submission, it would be appropriate for Mr. Zaric to explain to the Trial Chamber during his examination-in-chief what this certain criteria was. It's a matter which is more appropriate, in my submission, to be dealt with now than in cross-examination, as he has raised it and left it unanswered in his own evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Zaric can explain that, because that is his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've understood the objection of my learned colleague. Could you explain what you meant by "criteria," the word "criteria" that you've mentioned? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I was able to feel after the very first days, and when I was going to the public security station, I meant what are the criteria which were used in order to detain people, and I got the following information: It is because they were possessing illegal weapons, and this is why they were detained. And their names were on the list of the war plan which belonged to that service, and those people were deployed in some paramilitary units. However, and I do not want to go in depth as to what are the criteria. Mr. Todorovic was establishing those. If I were a man and chief of the public security station and if I were an important man, I don't know if I would apply the same criteria. But I wanted to say: Aside from the fact that they had spoken about it, it was very clear, very soon, and we were able to see that the prisons were full of people who neither had any weapons nor whose names were on those lists. So when I talk about that verbal disagreement, I always -- actually, I meant that, and this is why I'm also mentioning the name of Esref Zaimbegovic, Dragan Delic [Realtime transcript read in error omitted words "Dragan Delic"], and others who were brought, according to me, without any reason and what kept in custody for months and months on end in various prisoners and detention centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we just have the name of Dragan Delic. I believe that we all heard this name while Mr. Zaric was giving his testimony, and I haven't seen this in transcript. Because when he was referring to people that according to his position were arrested with no good reason, the name of Esref Zaimbegovic was mentioned but also the name of Dragan Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is agreed that it was mentioned. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us if Mr. Stevan Todorovic allowed anybody to leave the Detention Centre? Did he agree to your plea?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I think that my interventions had a counter-effect. And after those -- or immediately after those interventions, these people for whom I had intervened actually had a worse treatment than before my interventions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in the barracks at Brcko, did you see a witness, Witness N?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do not mention his name, please. I am talking about the witness that I mentioned earlier on.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you speak to him at that point, or when you saw him then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, only briefly. We had about half an hour, or I had about half an hour to talk to all the detainees whenever I would go to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: After that brief conversation, did you make any notes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know a man - he's a citizen of Bosanski Samac and he's known as Kemal Mehinovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very well, but I do know him from sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever talk to Savo Djurdjevic? He was a police officer on service. And did you ever tell him that somebody was beating up Kemal Mehinovic -- here somebody else should beat Mr. Mehinovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that Mr. Mehinovic was in prison up until some documents were disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no idea that Mr. Mehinovic was in prison, and it is only after some documents of the Prosecution were disclosed when I came on my own free will to The Hague. I had not received any communications. I have not seen -- had not seen that man in prison. I had not had any conversations with this man. And I would never have asked anybody to apply any kinds of measures towards him or anybody else. That would be the only detainee that I would have intervened for. So I never, ever intervened for anybody, and I didn't even know that he was in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever tell any police officer at the police station in Samac--

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, because the transcript was not quite clear. Because here it says: "So I never, ever intervened for anybody." And this would probably cause some misunderstanding, because Mr. Zaric was a couple of minutes ago talking about his interventions made to Mr. Todorovic, to do something about certain detainees to be released from the detention. So just if this can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, a few moments ago you talked about Mr. Mehinovic. It was not too clear in the transcript as to what you said regarding Mr. Mehinovic. What did you say, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I never asked any police officer whatsoever to do anything, to apply any measures regarding Mr. Mehinovic, and I did not know that Mr. Mehinovic was in detention in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever ask any police officer in the police station of Bosanski Samac to beat up any detainee detained at the police officer [as interpreted] or to apply force?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Quite to the contrary; whenever I had the opportunity, I said the contrary, especially when I was talking to police officers who were not newly arrived and who were not the yes man of Stevan Todorovic and I was always encouraging them to behave correctly towards those men. That's the only thing that they could have ever heard from Simo Zaric whenever I would go and pay a visit to that police station. That is quite rare, actually, even if that's the main reason for my being at the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever use the telephone at the police station of Bosanski Samac to talk to somebody regarding some exchanges?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never with anybody on that subject. I did not discuss exchanges with anybody, neither from the public security station and neither from any other place, and everything I said, I maintain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know Mrs. Snjezana Delic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Mrs. Snjezana Delic from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe ten years prior to the war. She was a young woman then. Then she was a professor. She was working at the school centre and she was one of the professors, one of the teachers who taught my son Mirel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know whose wife she was, who she was married to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was married to Dragan Delic, who was the president of the management board of Mebos. It's a company in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know Hasan Delic, the father of Dragan Delic and the father-in-law of Snjezana Delic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him very well, Mr. Hasan is of an older generation. He's older than me. But he is a man who, up until his retirement, worked in the public security station, and this is how I knew him. But I also knew him as a member of the Second World War defence -- he participated in the Second World War, and I used to see him a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what were your -- what was your relationship with him and with the father?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the relationship was very friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some small misunderstanding here in the transcript on page 55, line 9. The question that Mr. Pisarevic posed was: What was your relationship with him? Referring to Hasan Delic, father of Dragan Delic. And then Mr. Zaric replied to that question. So this is -- the way it was recorded here might suggest that about some relation between father and son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't see that myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Your Honour, on page 55, line 9, here it says: "Mr. Zaric --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What was he describing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- "What was your relationship with him and with the father"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Was it a relationship between Mr. Zaric and the son, and then the relationship between Mr. Zaric and the father?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He was talking about Mr. Hasan Delic, the father --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe we can just go over it. Yes. So we come -- we deal with it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what was your relationship with Hasan Delic? How would you describe that relationship?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My relationship with Hasan Delic, Dragan's father, was very correct, even friendly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, during the war, were you in Dragan's and Snjezana's house?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did that come about? How did you find yourself in the Delic's house?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief when I explain this, but before I give you my answer, I have to give you one fact. Dragan Delic, Hasan's son and Snjezana's husband, had been arrested. That was in mid-April. I don't know the exact date. And he was brought to the public security station in Bosanski Samac. And I know very well that he was one of the people who were transferred to Brcko with the group who went there. I also know that Dragan Delic then was returned from Bijeljina to the area of Samac. That was again in mid-May. And since our former friendship, Hasan Delic, his father, was very concerned about the lot of his two sons. Dragan was in the prison, and the other son, Hazim, had a work obligation. So I understood him as a parent. He tried to see whether I, on my part, could do something about Dragan, to see whether I could have Dragan released from prison. What I could do through the people who worked in the crime department, I could ask them about the reasons why Dragan had been detained, and I received information from Milos Savic, who told me that Dragan Delic had been charged, together with some people from Mebos, of having abused the funds of that company for illegal arming of Muslims in Bosanski Samac, also that they had formed a work group consisting of accountants who went to Mebos, made an analysis, and decided that the books were cooked. I carelessly --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Again we have some small misunderstanding. Here on page 57 it says that after this group of bookkeepers or accountants checked the records of Mebos factory, they find out - that is Mr. Zaric said - that it has nothing to do with truth. But here it says: "And decided that the books were cooked."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think he can -- Mr. Zaric can give us that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team of financial experts which went on Milos Savic's instructions - that's my information - checked the allegations and issued a written report and stated that Dragan Delic did not participate in any financial [indiscernible], nor the financial funds had ever been used for illegal arming of Muslims, and this is what I wanted to say. And it is this precise information that I conveyed to Mr. Hasan when I received this information, and that was -- I can't remember exactly when, but it was sometime in June. And I told him that I believed that everything would be all right, because I had heard that Dragan had nothing whatsoever to do with the type of crime that he was charged with. Hasan, as a father, went again to the public security station and said to Mr. Todorovic that he had heard from me, which was a fact, he said: Simo Zaric told me that my son was not guilty, that he didn't do what you say he did. That's why I had problems with Stevo. Stevo told me that I disclosed information to a balija, and I don't want to use any more of the terms that he used. And despite all that, Stevo did not want to release Dragan Delic, against whom there were no grounds whatsoever to keep him in prison. In late June, in the evening, Hasan Delic found me and told me: Simo, I need to talk to you about something important, but can you come to my place when it gets dark? And he also told me: But I won't be in my apartment. Mr. Hasan lived in a different part of the town. I will be in Snjezana's apartment. Dragan Delic had a house in where his wife, Snjezana, resided together with his two children. I said to Hasan that I would be there in the evening, and that's exactly what I did. That's how I visited the Delic family, and I found Hasan, Snjezana, and her two children in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about, and what did you learn from them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some bad news from them. The first thing that I learned was from Snjezana, who told me that during that day, Mr. Blagojevic had paid her a visit, that is, Mr. Stojan Blagojevic, and that he was looking for some other women with whom he had an interview, and that he also had an interview with her, and that he was surprised that she did not have a work obligation, and that he also told her that early on the following day she should report to the Tekstilac company, where she would be working. The Tekstilac company was a factory where the production had started, and there was also a restaurant where ladies were cooking meals for the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you then also learn that Mr. Stojan Blagojevic had confiscated Dragan Delic's passenger vehicle?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me that the vehicle had been confiscated, and they showed me a document about that vehicle. I don't know whether it was a Yugo or a 101, but if I were to see this document, I could remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: It is not important.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, this vehicle had been confiscated on that day, and it was confiscated by Mr. Stojan Blagojevic, who was accompanied by Mr. Aco Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell Mrs. Snjezana Delic in the presence of her father-in-law, Hasan Delic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told her that, as far as I knew, that the women with young children, and her children were under the age of 10 - I don't know how old they were, but they were young, in any case - that these women could not have a work obligation and that this was the position when it came to the work obligation, and that I would talk to some people from the Ministry of Defence and I would check that. And as far as the vehicle was concerned, I told her that I didn't know anything about that, but the document that she had received, I told her that she should keep it and maybe in the foreseeable future you could be able to either return the car or you could be compensated for the possible damage. That is what I told her in the presence of her father-in-law, Mr. Hasan Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So what about her work obligation? Did she have to comply with that obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she did not have that obligation, because she had young children who were very young. And on the following day, I talked to Mr. Milos Bogdanovic about that. He told me then: Simo, I'm leaving the secretariat, but in any case, I can tell you that this is not possible, and Stojan Blagojevic does not have the authority to order anybody to have a work obligation. I asked him to do something vis-a-vis Stojan Blagojevic and tell him that it was not his place to get involved in that. Later on, I heard that Snjezana did not go to that factory and that she did not have a work obligation, so I assume that Mr. Blagojevic did receive a certain instruction to the effect that this was not up to him to order anybody to do work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 12.50 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know the person called Esma Fitozovic from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know her.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever, during 1992, have any sort of conversation with her?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not an official one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you ever order her to report to the police station in Bosanski Samac every day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you went to the police station, did you ever see Mrs. Esma Fitozovic there in the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only once in one of the offices of the crime department on the upper floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you never had an official conversation with her, what were your private conversations about, when you had an opportunity to talk to her? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our conversations were brief. I know Mrs. Esma Fitozovic rather well, and since I had an opportunity to talk to Mr. Milos Savic and Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic and receive information that the members of the police had searched her apartment, and on that occasion they had found over 30 kilogrammes of explosives under her mattress and some other material. That's why she was asked to come for an interview, to the police station. At the moment when we were together in one of those offices, I told her: Esma, how is it possible for you to allow this to take place? How could you sleep on so much explosives? Her reply to me was: Don't ask me anything, Simo. I swear by my children that I don't have an idea what my husband had done. He has fled, and he has abandoned me and my children. And that was the end of all the conversation between me and Mrs. Esma Fitozovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When she said "my husband," she meant Mr. Alija Fitozovic, who was one of the witnesses before this Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But there is one more thing in the transcript. Because Mr. Zaric was referring -- it was -- it's all right. It's now been corrected. I'm sorry. No. I apologise again. Here on page 61, on line 14, it says: "Our conversations were brief." And Mr. Zaric was talking in singular about that one and only conversation that he had with her. So this could maybe provoke some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But he has explained as to what he discussed with her during -- at the police station. So we can proceed, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know a citizen of Bosanski Samac, Esref Kapetanovic? Let me remind you. Esref Kapetanovic, also known as major's son [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him. For a brief moment I could not remember who you were talking about, but I do know this lad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Esref Kapetanovic, in May 1992, ask you for some assistance?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came to my apartment and we had a brief conversation in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did he want from you? What did he ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He briefly informed me that Jelena Kapetanovic, whose last name was Stanisic at that time, they lived together. He said that she had been isolated, that she was in Crkvina, and he asked me if I could help him and have Jelena released from that isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you reply to him, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him: I have no authority whatsoever, but my suggestion to him was that he should go to the Red Cross and see if these people could help him, primarily to see why Jelena, being a female, had been isolated. And then he told me: I went to the Red Cross, and their answer to me was rather inconclusive, very ambiguous. And then I said to Mr. Kapetanovic: I'm very sorry, but at this moment, I can't help you with that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, at any point, through the radio communication, did you negotiate about the exchange of some pilots?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no pilots, or anything along these lines. That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know a citizen of Bosanski Samac called Kemal Bobic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you say to Sejdin [as interpreted], Naser, known as Cakar that he should arrest Kemal Bobic, and he was a police officer at the station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, neither Bobic or anyone else. That's my one and only answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever have an opportunity to see Kemal Bobic, who had been beaten up and was in the office of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I did hear that he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on the 17th of April, 1992, did you participate in the collection of weapons in the building in which you lived and which was known as number 62?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, in Vuk Karadzic Street in Bosanski Samac, did you ever participate in the unloading of weapons from a truck to the house of Mustafa Omeranovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a lie. My sister and my brother-in-law live there, but this is just a fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may we now move into private session, because we will talk about a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I would like to talk about your family, Mr. Zaric. You have told us so far that on the 16th of April, 1992, in the afternoon hours, that you were in your mother's house in Trnjak and that this is why you were late to the meeting of the municipality, the local commune of Bosanski Samac, and it was the meeting of the coordination body. Tell us, please: Talking about the estate where your mother lives, whose estate was this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This estate belonged to my father, and he had -- I had inherited that estate. But through a decision of the court, while my mother was alive, she was to benefit from it, to live on there, and then my sisters too. But while my father was still alive, I was the only male member of the Zaric family, so I inherited the whole estate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you take care of that estate?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you also take care of your mother?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially I took care of my mother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think we've been through this evidence before, and constantly you talk about travelling to go and see his mother and [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is partially the fact, because the witness only partially testified on this. But I would like Mr. Zaric to talk to us about the fact as to where his mother was on the 16th, 17th, 18th, and the 19th of April. I believe that this is important and pertinent for the defence of Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but he can deal with that, but we also have his evidence as to where he, Mr. Zaric, was during those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Please tell us: How old was your mother at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother was around 70 years old at the time. She was in her late 70s and she was about to turn 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your mom live on that estate in the village of Trnjak in Sava ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Not quite accurate. "She was in her late 70s and she was about to turn 80." This is not the situation. This is not what Mr. Zaric said. He said: My mother had recently her birthday, her 80th birthday, so she wasn't something like 70 years old.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You have explained, Mr. Lazarevic, so we can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that evening, Mr. Zaric, the evening of the 16th of April, 1992, did your mother, Mileva, remain in the village of Trnjak, part of the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She stayed in Trnjak. She was always alone in the house. And on the 16th, in the evening, she stayed there. She was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when did your mom leave the village of Trnjak, and when did she leave the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She left on the 19th of April, 1992, in the morning hours. It was the Catholic Easter. Thanks to the fact that she was picked up by the husband of my youngest sister, Nada. His name is Marko Jakic. He is a Croatian by nationality and he was able to go through all the barricades and the checkpoints. And thanks to him, my mother was able to leave Trnjak. On that same day, in the afternoon, together with the brother-in-law, Marko, with Nada and their child, they left the estate, and it was then, that afternoon, that my estate was the first estate to be burnt down on the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did your mother go with your son-in-law, your sister, and their child?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to the territory of Serbia. Then another sister came to join them. Mara Brocilovic, from Odzak, had joined them with her family, and then my mother and all of them together lived for a while in Uzika Pozega, in Serbia, not far from a place called Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: During 1992, did your mother ever have the opportunity to go back to Bosanski Samac? Did she ever come back to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did. My mother did go back to the territory of the municipality of Samac and Odzak, towards mid-August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in Bosanski Samac, where did she stay after she came back?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She stayed at the house in which my daughter got married, my daughter Natasa. This was the house of Djuro Prgomet. And after her arrival, I went to see the competent body of the Municipal Assembly, headed by Mr. Veso Blagojevic, and I obtained a document stating that that house was put at my mother's disposal, my mother and also two other kums who were with her at the time. And she unfortunately stayed for a very short period of time there, because she was actually evicted from that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So your mother was staying at the house of her granddaughter, Natasa; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You've just stated a few moments ago that your mother was evicted from the house in which she was staying, the house of Natasa, her granddaughter and your daughter. How did that come about? Why was she evicted, and what did you do? Which measures did you take so that the eviction does not take place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in November, sometime in November. I was already working on the territory of the municipality of Pelagicevo. I got the information that the police arrived, that they were evicting my mother. I immediately got in my car and arrived -- went to Samac. When I got there, in front of the building, I saw a police officer -- four police cars and police officers, and I saw Mrs. Vajagic, Joka. She had come on behalf of the organs to tell my mother and my kums who were there that they should leave the house. So then I called Mr. Blagoje Simic, the president of the War Presidency, and I kindly requested and asked him not to do this to me, because everything that I had in Trnjak was burnt down and my mother doesn't have a place to go. So Mr. Blagoje told me that there was an assembly of the War Presidency going on and that he was trying to do his best in order to make sure that she is not evicted. He told me to call him back in an hour or two. I told him, or I told, rather, the police officers, that I had a conversation with him and to wait. Then an hour or two later I called Mr. Blagoje Simic, but he told me: Simo, the War Presidency voted 4 versus 3, so there were 7 in the War Presidency, and the decision was adopted that this should take place, that my mother and that these people had to leave the house. So I asked Blagoje if it was possible to take something from that house. I had a dining-room set. It was a carved wood dining-room set and I had bought that set to my daughter when she got married. And Blagoje told me: Yes, you can take whatever you think you should take. And then a commission would come, a commission who was going to do all the inventory. And then another man came, a man who worked at an office, and then he worked there earlier, and I had heard from him that he had gotten a house in Zasavica. So there was absolutely no good reason for such a thing to occur. But he was from Zavidovici. He was a member of the SDS. His rating was much higher than my mother and the other people who had no place to live. And then I had to move them in unfortunately a rundown house in Tihici of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who this house in Tihici belonged, whom it belonged to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the house of the parents of Mr. Sulejman Tihic. So then I made sure that I had put some kind of makeshift plastic windows, and that's how I tried to resolve my mother's fate. And it is only when this Honourable Trial Chamber in the year 2000 released me and gave me provisional release, it is only then when I went to Samac that I was able to take care of my mother on a better basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you get the information from Blagoje Simic that he really tried to do his best?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I really know when I got the information from Blagoje Simic that he was trying to do his best, that my mother stay, Mr. Mirko Lukic and Mr. Sincic, I don't know however if Sincic at the time was at a very high level. I don't know if he was a member -- a very high level member of the War Presidency, but I know that he was present at the meeting. All the other members that were there next to Mr. Blagoje showed that they were powerful within that War Presidency. And even today, in spite of everything, I do not doubt that Mr. Blagoje Simic tried to do everything in his power to make my mother stay there. But I think that, unfortunately, he was surrounded with players with whom he -- to whom he could not command and he could not have any influence on the other participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, today, in the year 2003, what is the status of your mother?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She is a displaced person in Trnjak, where I was born and where my estate was. Nobody has returned there. My fellow villagers of Trnjak are waiting for me to return, and then they all follow suit. And my mother is living with one sister and then with another sister. And then when my wife, she stays with them, a month with one, two months with another, and that seems to be her destiny.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell this Honourable Trial Chamber: What happened with your property, with your assets?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My assets have all disappeared. It happened in the course of one afternoon. Everything was burnt to the ground. Only some tractors and machinery remained. I had one of the biggest orchards in Posavina. And as far as my house and outbuildings are concerned, all this has burnt down. All this burnt down in the course of one afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have just mentioned the agricultural machinery. What happened to that machinery?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was confiscated while the HVO and the Muslim forces controlled Odzak and that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would now like to ask to present to Mr. Zaric and Honourable Trial Chamber four photographs depicting the assets of Mr. Zaric, and another photo -- actually, two photos depicting the monument which had been erected in the village of Dubica, to the memory of the victims of fascism in the Second World War. We have already given those photos to our learned friends from the Prosecutor's office. Or maybe it would be more practical for us to make a break and continue talking about this after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have our break and continue our proceedings at 1445. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I please ask the usher to put the photographs, to have them prepared for the Trial Chamber and for Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pisarevic, on your photographs, you can discuss the photographs showing Mr. Zaric's property, but the photograph showing the monument for those who perished in the Second World War will not be allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since we were told that the Prosecution were given the photographs, is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, is this part of the outbuildings in your farm?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What do we see here? What are these outbuildings that have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm showing now is the building which used to house pigs. This part here, this used to be a dry kiln for meat. And here there are two columns and there are four more on the right-hand side. Behind that, there was a big barn that served for fodder and part of the farm mechanisation. From this building here, to the right, there was a large outbuilding which also served to house a mechanisation and barrels for the fruit, but this all burnt to the ground. So you can't see those outbuildings, because they completely perished in the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the second photo on the ELMO, please. Is this again part of your property?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is one of the buildings in the farm. This part that I'm showing right now was used as a kitchen. That's what my mother most often used. This used to be a garage, and the part that can't be seen here without a window, that used to be a larder. And on top here, this used to be a completely new floor with a staircase on the southern part. This used to be a beautiful, new building that was built immediately before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we see the third photo. And can you tell us what you can see here.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the family house that belonged to me and to my parents, and here, in the part that I'm showing right now, in the year 1995, I constructed a new concrete floor, and there was the attic part on top of it. This all burnt. I did not have the time to finish it, to complete it. Here, where you can see the brick wall, between the brick wall and the window here, there used to be a staircase which led to the top floor, which was 11 by 11 metres large.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And now let's see the fourth photo. What can we see here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the larger outbuildings. Here you can see a metal part. From here, downwards, there was a metal staircase for the attic, and you can see the attic door here. What I would like to say is that this hall here that you can see in the wall, this is a hall on the southern wall, a result of the shelling from a recoilless gun from the village of Prud. This shell pierced through four walls and reached the very far end of the building. This same happened on the western side of the building. It seems that they were testing the power of their artillery on this building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek some clarification. It seems a little bit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just seek some clarification. It seems a little unclear. Mr. Zaric just referred to 1995. Perhaps if we could find out when the photographs were taken and when the damage was done. I'm just not quite following it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, yes. When the estate was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's right. When the photos -- whether they're recent photos or contemporaneous photos. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But is there any dispute from the Prosecution that his family estate was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. It's just it's unclear, because he mentioned 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to know whether it was before or after the events in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I mentioned 1995 in connection with this building, it was not this building. I was talking about the large family house where, in 1995, I had constructed a new concrete ceiling. This house was in this state in 1992. And if you look at it today, you will see that it still looks the same as it does in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was your property destroyed, I mean your farm, in 1992, as we see on these buildings?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This happened in 1992. It was set on fire on the 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, who was on the territory of the village of Trnjak? Or rather, what were you doing in 1995 in connection with your damaged family house?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to put a new roof on the old family house so that my mother could go and live there, not knowing what would happen towards the end of 1995 and that certain political decisions would be made whereby this part of the village of Trnjak would come to belong to the Federation, which, for the people living there, meant that they definitely had to leave. In 1995, when I had gathered enough funds, I tried to repair the house so that my mother could continue living there and so that I could visit from time to time and continue helping my mother and restore the farm to a normal state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in 1995, did you succeed in improving your property?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, apart from the concrete slab on top of the house and some brick work, I didn't manage to do anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could these exhibits be given numbers, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This set of four photographs will be treated as Exhibit D55/4, in the order they were introduced, from A to D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to Their Honours, but I know that Her Honour Judge Mumba said that the photographs of the monuments should not be exhibited. But may I say something about those pictures and that monument?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, those are matters concerning the Second World War. I'm aware that you did discuss what happened to your family, but that was sufficient. We don't need to discuss anything anymore concerning the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you testified here that your sisters, Mara, Jelena, and Nada, lived in the town of Odzak. Tell us: When did your sisters leave the town of Odzak? What was the date?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but after the 19th, a few days later, they left, and thanks to some friends and neighbours of theirs, non-Serbs, in Odzak, who helped them leave - for example, my sister, Jelena managed to leave because she put on a Muslim woman's costume, and thus she passed through a checkpoint. A Muslim friend of hers took her to an area where she could reach the part inhabited by Serbs. My sister Mara and my brother-in-law Nenad left in a similar way, thanks to friends, non-Serbs, who helped them get out of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. You said that they left after the 19th. What month and what year was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in April 1992, immediately after the 19th of April, perhaps between the 19th and the 25th of April. That was the week when all my sisters managed to leave Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Mr. Zaric, as a member of the JNA, did you have any kind of relations with the SDS political party in the municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had no relations with the SDS party on behalf of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether the command of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA had any relations with the SDS political party in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of anything that would be official contacts, but I do know that Commander Nikolic sometimes said that he had talked to some people from the SDS, some people from the HDZ, some people from the SDA, so at that level he did have certain talks, and I heard about that from time to time. But as for some sort of official support by the command of the 17th Tactical Group for the political party of the SDS, I had no information about that whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. During your testimony, Mr. Zaric, you mentioned Stevan Todorovic several times. Can you tell us how you knew Mr. Stevan Todorovic before the outbreak of hostilities in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him slightly. I knew him from the pre-war days as an administrator of a factory, and those of us who knew about the economy and business did not have a high opinion of him as a businessman. With the help of some friends, however, he was appointed receiver of a factory, of a furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any friendly relations with him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would see each other from time to time, but we would only say hello. He was a young man who liked cafe life. He liked socialising. And I never imagined, on the basis of his leisurely and informal behaviour before the war that he would turn out the way he did during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I was just waiting for the interpretation to finish. I just think it's a point of clarification. This seems rather a new term for us to hear about Mr. Todorovic. Maybe it's a translation issue. Page 85, line 5: "He was appointed receiver of a factory." Is this the correct term, "receiver"? Receivers are usually to do with bankruptcy and so on and so forth. I'm just wondering whether we could clarify what exactly the position was, to make sense of the record.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time he was the receiver and he was preparing for the bankruptcy proceedings of that factory. So you are correct, Your Honour. The factory was bankrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what were your relations with Stevan Todorovic during the war on the territory of Bosanski Samac, or, more precisely, from the 17th of April, 1992, until the end of the war in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our relations were quite bad. Almost from the very first days of the outbreak of hostilities until the end of the war, Stevan Todorovic was really quite a character. He was a man who, when he gained power, assumed a completely different role, a role in which one could not recognise him any more. No normal communication with him was possible. He did not take into account any advice. He advocated Serb nationalism. He advocated positions I disliked. And the way he treated detainees is something that need not be commented on here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you and your family have any problems with Mr. Todorovic, or rather, the police organ whose chief he was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very often. My wife mentioned one of these incidents. I will not repeat this. But Mr. Todorovic was very rough with me. He set up an arrest for me and Mr. Fadil Topcagic at Rasa, where we were taken to the police station in Sremska Mitrovica, on the territory of Serbia, under suspicion that we were illegally transferring Croats and Muslims to Serbia, and people later told us, when they learned who Simo Zaric was and what sort of man I was, they told us about this. Secondly, as chief of the public security station, he arrested my son on several occasions, brought him in and exposed him to very unpleasant situations. For example, on one occasion, they took him from a wedding my son was attending, and this man was dressed up as if he was Draza Mihajlovic. There were open threats which I heard from others that he had uttered. But I never trembled before him, although I was afraid that one day it might cost me my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you and Mr. Stevan Todorovic ever plan, prepare, incite, order, or aid and abet, or support the planning, preparation, or perpetration of persecutions of the population on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Something like that could never happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Zaric, would you please tell us what your relations were with Milan Simic before the war.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war I had relatively good relations with Milan Simic. I knew him as an economist younger than me. When I was the director of the company he worked in my accounting department in Buducnost. Before that, I knew that he worked in other companies and that he was considered to be quite an expert in accounting. He was a calm person, a friendly person, one with whom you could discuss many topics in a very reasonable manner. I knew his father Vojin better than I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how well did you know Mr. Milan Simic, and what were your relations during the war, during 1992 until the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, of all the people I knew before the war whose characteristics were good, if one of them showed many bad characteristics during the war, Mr. Milan Simic is one of them, and I'm deeply disappointed in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any relations with him during the war?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a few skirmishes, and in the presence of Mr. Todorovic, I have to say that for I don't know what reasons, Milan started drinking frequently at the beginning of the war, and he was holding a very responsible and important post. He and Todorovic attacked me after the announcement, after the move to Brcko, when I was in the command of the brigade, at a meeting Mr. Simic insulted me so badly that many people got up to calm him down. He thought I was a frustrated man, someone who was behind the times, and so on. And my greatest disappointment was what Mr. Milan, as the president of the government, allowed himself to do, and that was to dispense justice to helpless people in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you, together with Mr. Milan Simic, ever plan, prepare, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aid and abet the planning, preparation, or execution of any persecution of the non-Serbian population in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Simo Zaric was never part of that group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us since when you have known Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got to know him a few days before the start of the war. He was one of the younger intellectuals on the territory of Bosanski Samac. I knew his brother, Cedomir, much better, because I worked with him, and of course his father, and I knew Blagoje as a promising young doctor, who was said to be one of the better students of the school of medicine at the university and who worked in the health centre in Bosanski Samac and raised some important issues concerning dialysis, which was a big problem in our area. In the late autumn of 1991, he and his family moved to the building in which I also lived, so from then on I saw him more often. However, we only said hello and greeted each other. We never sat down in a cafe together, or anywhere else, to have a drink together, which would mean that we were friends rather than simply acquaintances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Blagoje Simic ever come to your apartment? Did he ever visit you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Blagoje Simic never came to my apartment, nor did he visit any other member of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever go to Mr. Blagoje Simic's apartment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never went to his place, nor did any other member of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Line 9 and 10. Mr. Zaric answered: "Mr. Blagoje Simic never came to my apartment, nor did any other of his family." And here it says: "Nor did he visit any other members of my family."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll accept your correction, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What were your relations like with Mr. Blagoje Simic during the course of the war, from 1992 up until 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aside from the fact that we had some political differences, ideologically we were on different wavelengths. Mr. Blagoje Simic and myself, we could say that we had relation -- we had a relationship which tolerated each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever plan, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aid and abet the planning, preparation, or execution of any crime referred to in -- previously, such as the prosecution of the people of the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter notes: With Mr. Blagoje Simic? Answer: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I think we also need a little clarification of the text here, transcript, page 90, line 3. It talks about the prosecution of the people of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. I presume you're talking about what's in the indictment, persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. Yes, the persecution of the non-Serb population of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known him for a longer period of time. He is 10 or 11 years older than me. He belongs to a different generation. When I was a younger man, he always remained in my memory as being a very good athlete on the territory of -- in the territory of Novi Grad municipality of Odzak. Later on, he became a professor. He worked at the mechanical, technical school, and at the time I was attending the secondary school of economics. So I've known Mr. Tadic ever since I was a younger man. But at the time, Mr. Tadic and myself were not particularly good friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was your relationship like with Mr. Tadic, meaning before the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of October, 1991, when I had to retire and when, because of my retirement, I had more free time, I started to go to the Cafe AS, where I had the opportunity to play pool and to talk to some people, to play cards with some friends, and this is how and when I met more often Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic ever come to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Tadic never came to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, tell us: Aside from the fact that you were going to Cafe AS, did you ever pay a visit to Mr. Miroslav Tadic's house?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it was on one occasion only. It was a birthday party, and a friend of mine, an old school friend, came to Mr. -- Jovisa Kovacevic. Mr. Tadic invited me and this man, and I believe that only once I went to his apartment. It was on a first floor. And I never visited him otherwise. He was not a friend in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever plan, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aid and abet the planning, the preparation or execution of the non-Serb population - sorry - the persecution of the non-Serb population of the municipality of Bosanski Samac with Mr. Miroslav Tadic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you, in concert with any other person, plan, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aid and abet the planning, the preparation, or the persecution of the non-Serb population of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everything I did was quite the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you plan, instigate, order, commit, or otherwise aid and abet the planning, the preparation, or the execution of the illegal deportation and transfer -- and forcible transfer of hundreds of Bosnian Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and other non-Serb civilians, including women, children, and the elderly, from their homes of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, and did you participate in their transfer to other countries and other parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were not under the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It has nothing to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. Can you please tell us when and how did you find out that there was an indictment against you and that you were figuring amongst a list of accused for the criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found this -- I found about this at the end of July 1995. I was at the time on the battlefield with my unit, in the municipality of Lopare.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Lopare is situated where, approximately?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Lopare is situated to the east of Bijeljina, in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How far is that from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Bosanski Samac, one could say that going through Bijeljina and Zvornik, maybe there's 150 kilometres between -- in between, or more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when did you decide to voluntarily give yourself up and to put yourself under the custody of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, for crimes committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took this decision at the very moment when I felt that, in the territory of the Republika Srpska, political activities were created in such a way that this was possible; otherwise, I would have come earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was stopping you, Mr. Zaric, from giving yourself up and putting yourself under the custody of the Tribunal? What were these security political reasons for which you couldn't give yourself up immediately and put yourself under the custody of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say: It is only in 1996, if I remember correctly, after the Dayton Agreement, that the first conditions were created and that the first after-war elections were able to take place. Through these elections, and up until actually that time, the political monopoly or, should I say, the SDS was holding the monopoly, and its political activities was creating some security components in such a way that they were not enabling me to come to this decision and to give myself up voluntarily to the Tribunal in The Hague. In 1993 I was particularly in favour of the creation of this Tribunal, never thinking that I would be sitting right now here. But when I'm talking about this, I would like to say that in this joint indictment which, for the first time, was published officially in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through all the media, I must say that there was five names from Bosanski Samac were on that list and Slobodan Miljkovic, Lugar, from Serbia, was also on the group of indictees, and on this list at that time I should say were some important people from the political and military life of Bosnia-Herzegovina, such as Mr. Karadzic, such as General Mladic, Dario Kordic, Mr. Aleksovski, and so on and so forth, other important personalities, their names were also on that list. A certain political climate was created, rallies, support rallies were organised, in favour of the people who were on those lists. This was all organised by the official authorities of the time, and I remember that such a rally took place in 1996 in Bosanski Samac, organised by the SDS, and the speakers who participated in that meeting at the cinema, which was full, I attended that meeting because I was interested by what was going on. They were defending the position of the people who were indicted and whose name appeared on that list of indictees. I recall that the very famous lawyer, Veljko Guberina, took the floor. I know that there was also Jovic, a political figure from Serbia. There were also some local leaders as well. But I will always remember the speech of the president of the municipality of Samac at the time, Mrs. Mirko Lukic, who replaced Mr. Blagoje, because Blagoje Simic was no longer appearing, because his name was also on the list of indictees, through a decision of the international community. Mr. Lukic was supporting Mr. Karadzic and Mladic and he was saying that those were important Serbian sons and that we should not -- or that they should not be delivered to anybody. He also started to talk about the situation, a local situation. Then he talked about us Serbs from the municipality of Samac. He talked about the people who were indicted. And I must say: That person had a very inflamed speech and he used a particular iconography, to mention Mr. Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Mr. Milan Simic. But he did not mention the names of Mr. Miroslav Tadic and myself. At that meeting, there were some divisions were created, some divisions were created, and there was a support given through an applause, a fiery applause, and Mirko Lukic, the president of the municipality, repeated again the names of those three men but myself and Mr. Tadic were not mentioned once again. And I recall correctly when I went to The Hague, I told Mr. Lukic that I will never forgive them for this, not because I want to be in the same basket as the other ones, but why are they making -- were they making such differences and thinking that we were less important [as interpreted] than the other ones? But I must say that such a political climate was not creating the necessary conditions for me to give myself up to the International Tribunal. I know that Mrs. Biljana Plavsic came, and I have my own personal opinions about her with regards to the responsibility, and when Mr. Dodik also public appeared and came. There were other political situations that were created. But this is why me and Mr. Tadic [as interpreted] took a decision to voluntarily give ourselves up to the Tribunal in The Hague, as the first Serbs who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have two corrections for the transcript. First is when Mr. Zaric said, on page 95, line 11: "And thinking that we were less" -- not important. He said less Serbs. This is what he said. And the other thing is that also Mr. Milan Simic was mentioned about making a decision to surrender them in the custody of the Tribunal, not just Mr. Tadic. So it's on page 95, line 17. This is why me and Mr. Tadic, as well as Mr. Milan Simic. Because he was also mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, we'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Zaric: You have given us your lawyers, Mr. Lazarevic and me, permission to express your apologies to every witness who was a victim of this war for everything that they suffered and they went through this war. Tell me, please, and tell this Honourable Chamber: What was your motive to give us such an order to express your regrets?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that I deemed as a human being was the least I could do to these people to express my sincere sympathy for the sufferings that they went through, because in a certain way I witnessed many things, I saw many things, I heard a lot of things as well. And I placed my all being to reduce the suffering to the minimum possible. Obviously I was powerless to prevent many of these things from happening. But when I asked you to express my words of sympathy for all these people went through, I meant that sincerely, as a human being, and before this Trial Chamber I would like to say that these are my sincere words from the bottom of my heart.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This completes my examination-in-chief of the witness Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something else before we continue? I would like to add a sentence to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really would not like to be misunderstood, but I find it very difficult to work like this. This is a superhuman effort for me. I have been testifying for some time now, and I feel rather tired. I don't know whether you have been informed that in the year 2000 I had undergone surgery and that I've been having a lot of problems. Before the beginning of my testimony, I asked my doctors to give me some sedatives to help me to endure and go through this battle, for which I've lived for the first -- last five years. I have the impression that I still have energy but not enough to allow me to be concentrated in the afternoon, at least not concentrated enough to be able to answer the important questions that will have a bearing on my destiny. That's why I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to consult my team of doctors and ask them whether I can endure such a long working day. I really feel very tired, very exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zaric. The Trial Chamber has understood what you have said. But then, between you and your lawyer, you asked for this long time to give evidence and to complete everything that you wanted to say. Because if you look at the record, the other two accused persons took this much time completing, including the cross-examination, upon their evidence, and the Trial Chamber had to allow you to take this much time just to make sure that you were given the rights that you needed to give evidence which you felt would help your defence. We shall now proceed to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber has decided that you'll take a break and we can continue with cross-examination tomorrow, and tomorrow we are sitting in the afternoon. I just want to find out who will start.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I don't have that many questions, I will be the first to start, and I believe it will take me about an hour to finish my cross-examination. And I assume that my colleague Pantelic will require more time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I see -- yes. I remember now the Trial Chamber has been informed that the two other witnesses are here, Mr. Erletic, I think, and Mr. Pantelic's witness. Maybe, to allow more time to Mr. Simo Zaric to rest, we can start with them tomorrow, because they're fairly short, I take it. And once we complete them, then the cross-examination can start. And also it will allow the other two witnesses to go back, instead of waiting. So we'll adjourn now and continue our proceedings tomorrow. Before we rise, Mr. Pantelic, I would like to find out: Would you like your witness to start tomorrow, or we start with Mr. Erletic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because your witness is also brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- I spoke with my learned friend Mr. Pisarevic. We think that maybe Mr. Erletic will start the cross-examination, and then have Mr. Pivasevic in-chief and additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So we shall start with Mr. Erletic, then. We will rise now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
